rounds.why: The windpipe, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. The open back of each ‘C’ lets the oesophagus bulge forward when you swallow a big mouthful.
Clear and flexible, it fine-tunes focus. It keeps adding layers all your life, like an onion, and slowly stiffens. Hello, reading glasses at 45.
The thigh bone: your longest and strongest. It’s roughly a quarter of your height, which is how forensic teams estimate stature from a single bone.

rounds.q: You knock your ‘funny bone’. Which nerve just zapped you?
rounds.why: Not funny, not a bone. The ulnar nerve sits just under the skin behind the elbow, so a knock fires off tingles into your ring and little fingers.
Your biggest internal organ and a full-time chemistry lab. It can regrow from about a quarter of its tissue, which is why living donors can give a slice.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: An S-shaped loop on a mobile mesentery, which is why it can twist (volvulus).
The veins that carry oxygenated blood: from lungs to left atrium. Usually four of them.
The tough white of the eye. It’s continuous with the clear cornea at the front.
The collarbone. It’s the first bone in the body to start hardening, around week five or six of pregnancy, and one of the most commonly broken bones in kids.
Wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled peanuts usually go right.
More mobile and more circular than the medial meniscus, so it’s injured less often.

rounds.q: Which bone is fractured most often in a fall on the outstretched hand, and can lose its blood supply?
rounds.why: Its blood enters from the far end, so a waist fracture can starve the near part. Snuffbox tenderness is the clue.
The kneecap: the body’s biggest sesamoid bone, meaning it grows inside a tendon. Babies have a cartilage version that only turns to bone at around three to six.
It equalises middle ear pressure. Shorter and flatter in children, which is one reason they get more ear infections.
A blood-rich layer feeding the outer retina. Its pigment helps absorb stray light.
No body and no spinous process. It holds up the skull, like the Titan Atlas.
The median nerve usually passes between its two heads, a spot where it can be compressed.

rounds.q: Which nerve runs through Guyon’s canal at the wrist?
rounds.why: Cyclists can compress it from leaning on handlebars: ‘handlebar palsy’.
The longest metacarpal, with the most rigid joint at its base. A stable post for pinching.
The largest vein in the body, carrying blood from the legs and abdomen.
The ‘hammer’, attached to the eardrum. You can often see its handle through an otoscope.

rounds.q: Winged shoulder blade when pushing against a wall. Which nerve?
rounds.why: It supplies serratus anterior, which pins the shoulder blade to the ribs. It runs long and exposed down the chest wall, so heavy backpacks and surgery can injure it.
The outflow valve of the right ventricle. The least likely of the four to cause trouble in adults.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the skin of the first web space on the top of the foot?
rounds.why: Its only skin patch. Numbness here can be an early sign of anterior compartment syndrome.

rounds.answer: Middle phalanx of the middle finger
wrong: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger
Distal phalanx of the middle finger
rounds.why: Each finger has three phalanges: proximal, middle and distal. The thumb has only two.
The first thoracic vertebra, carrying the first rib. Count down from C1 at the top.
Popliteus ‘unlocks’ the fully straightened knee, allowing it to bend.
The anvil, middle of the three ear bones. The ossicles are already close to adult size at birth, so they barely grow while the rest of you does.
Two leaflets between the left atrium and ventricle. It’s named because someone thought it looked like a bishop’s mitre. Yes, really.
Weak adductor pollicis makes you bend the thumb tip to grip paper: Froment’s sign.
A J-shaped muscle bag full of acid around pH 1 to 3. Its surface lining renews every few days so it doesn’t digest itself.

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve lets you smell?
rounds.why: Cranial nerve number one. Smell skips the thalamus relay that other senses use on the way in, one reason a smell can drag up a memory so fast.
The upper arm bone. It sounds like ‘humorous’, which is one theory for the name ‘funny bone’, though the zing is really the ulnar nerve.
Vision lives at the back of your head, about as far from your eyes as it gets. A hard knock there can make you literally ‘see stars’.
The receiving bay for blood coming back from the body. It houses the heart’s own pacemaker, the sinoatrial node.
Your main breathing muscle. Hiccups are it spasming, followed by the vocal cords snapping shut. That snap is the ‘hic’.
The light-sensing film at the back. It’s wired backwards: light passes through layers of nerve cells before it reaches the photoreceptors.
The shin bone and main weight-bearer of the lower leg. Its front edge sits right under the skin, which is why coffee tables hurt so much.
Stores and concentrates bile from the liver, then squeezes it out after a fatty meal. You can live perfectly well without one.
Snail-shaped (that’s literally the Greek). Unrolled it’s about 3 cm long. High pitches register at the base, low pitches at the tip.
Pea-sized and sitting on the front of the triquetrum. It’s a sesamoid bone inside a tendon.

rounds.q: After a shoulder dislocation: weak deltoid and a numb patch on the outer shoulder. Which nerve?
rounds.why: It wraps around the neck of the humerus, so dislocations stretch it. The numb ‘regimental badge’ patch, where a sleeve badge would sit, gives it away.
The first part of the large bowel. The appendix hangs from it.

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve moves the tongue?
rounds.why: Damage it and the tongue points towards the weak side when you stick it out.
The thumb-side forearm bone. It rolls around the ulna when you turn a doorknob, and it’s the usual wrist break after a fall on an outstretched hand.
The body’s main pipe, about as wide as your thumb. It rises out of the left ventricle, arches over the top and dives down behind the heart.
The clear front window, doing about two-thirds of the eye’s focusing. It has no blood vessels and takes much of its oxygen straight from the air.
The eardrum: about a tenth of a millimetre thick, thinner than paper. Small holes often heal on their own within a few weeks.

rounds.q: Which nerve gives feeling to the highlighted patch on the back of the hand?
rounds.why: The superficial branch of the radial nerve owns the back of the first web space. It’s the go-to spot for testing radial sensation after an upper arm fracture.

rounds.q: Which nerve can cause pain shooting down the back of the leg?
rounds.why: The body’s thickest nerve, about as wide as your thumb near its origin.
‘Hamate’ means hooked. Its hook can snap in golfers, cricketers and batters when the grip handle jams into the palm on a mistimed swing.

rounds.q: Foot drop after a tight plaster cast just below the knee. Which nerve?
rounds.why: It wraps around the neck of the fibula just under the skin, so casts, crossed legs and long squats can squash it.
The skinny outer leg bone. It carries little weight, so surgeons can borrow a length of it, with its blood supply, to rebuild a jaw.
Maybe not useless after all: it may act as a safe house for good gut bacteria. Its tip can point in lots of directions, which is why appendicitis pain can wander.
Front of the cross, hence ‘anterior’. Pop, swelling within hours, wobbly knee. Women footballers tear theirs two to eight times more often than men.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted strip of cortex.
rounds.why: The strip just in front of the central sulcus. It’s mapped upside down: feet near the top, face near the bottom, with huge areas for hands and lips.
It punches through coracobrachialis, powers elbow flexion, then ends as a skin nerve on the outer forearm. Hence ‘musculo’ plus ‘cutaneous’.
Thicker and stronger than the ACL. The classic tear is the ‘dashboard injury’: shin driven backwards in a car crash.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted organ, mostly hidden behind the stomach.
rounds.why: Its head nestles in the C-curve of the duodenum. It makes insulin plus over a litre of digestive juice a day, which is why pancreatitis is so nasty.
A ring of muscle that changes the lens shape so you can focus up close. It also makes aqueous humour, the fluid that keeps the front of your eye inflated.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the left lung.
rounds.why: The left lung has no middle lobe; this tongue-shaped part of the upper lobe does the job. ‘Lingula’ is Latin for little tongue.
The wall between the ventricles, and it pumps too. A hole here, a VSD, is one of the most common heart defects babies are born with.
Latin for ‘little brain’: about a tenth of brain volume, yet roughly four in five of its neurons. Neuroscientist Suzana Herculano-Houzel counted them by turning brains into soup.

rounds.answer: C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal
rounds.why: The hypoglossal is just the bus. The passengers are C1 spinal nerve fibres.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus?
wrong: Median nerve proper, in the palm
rounds.why: Lose it and you can’t make an ‘OK’ sign: the thumb and index tips go flat.
The parietal lobe handles touch, body position and spatial awareness.
Most people have 12 pairs. Pairs 11 and 12 ‘float’, with no attachment at the front.
The largest bone of the foot. The Achilles tendon attaches to it.
It receives oxygenated blood from the lungs. When it quivers in atrial fibrillation, clots can form in it.

rounds.q: How many bones does a typical adult skeleton have?
rounds.why: Babies start with more, around 270 to 300, which fuse as they grow.
C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open. The open part of the ‘C’ faces the oesophagus behind it.
Seven neck vertebrae, the same number as a giraffe.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the skeleton.
rounds.why: The adult cranium is several plates joined at sutures, still partly open as fontanelles in babies.
The auricle funnels sound in. Its folds help you tell whether a sound is in front or behind.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone at the knee.
rounds.why: The femur’s two rounded condyles rest on the flatter top of the tibia.
Five chunky vertebrae carrying most of your upper body weight. No ribs attach here, which is how you tell them from thoracic ones.
Roots L2 to L4. Tap the patellar tendon and you’re testing it: the knee jerk is mostly L3 and L4.
Fall on an outstretched hand, tender snuffbox: think scaphoid. Its blood supply enters from the far end, so a break across the middle can starve the near piece.
About 2.5 cm long. Wax and skin migrate outwards along it, so it cleans itself.
Carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. An artery carrying low-oxygen blood: the classic exam trap.
A C-shaped cartilage cushion on the inner side. It’s anchored to the joint capsule and MCL, so it moves less and tears more often than the lateral one.
The ulna sits on the little-finger side. Its tip is the point of your elbow (the olecranon).

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve moves the eye outwards, via lateral rectus?
rounds.why: Abducens abducts. Its long path along the base of the skull means raised brain pressure can stretch it and cause double vision.
Over a million fibres leave the eye here, creating a blind spot with no photoreceptors. Your brain quietly fills in the gap.
Hearing, memory and understanding language. ‘Temporal’ may come from tempus, time, because grey hairs often show first at the temples.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted area of the left hemisphere.
rounds.why: Damage here gives fluent but meaningless speech, with poor understanding.
The breastbone, where you push for CPR: lower half, 100 to 120 times a minute. Its tip, the xiphoid, may not fully turn to bone until middle age.
The L5/S1 disc is one of the two commonest to herniate, with L4/5.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius? (Lose it and the opposite hip drops when you stand on one leg.)
rounds.why: That hip drop is the Trendelenburg sign. A badly placed buttock injection is one way to injure this nerve, hence the upper outer quadrant rule.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the skin over the outer edge of the foot?
rounds.why: Surgeons often harvest it for nerve grafts. The trade-off is a small numb patch.
It includes the lingula, the tongue-shaped piece that hugs the heart.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the skin over the medial malleolus?
rounds.why: The longest branch of the femoral nerve, travelling with the great saphenous vein.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: It hangs across the abdomen from the hepatic flexure to the splenic flexure.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted nerve leaving the inner ear.
rounds.why: Hearing and balance. A benign tumour on it (vestibular schwannoma) causes one-sided hearing loss.

rounds.q: Brachioradialis flexes the elbow. Which nerve supplies it?
rounds.why: A classic trap: a flexor supplied by the extensor nerve.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted area of the left hemisphere.
rounds.why: In the left frontal lobe, for producing speech. Paul Broca’s famous patient was nicknamed ‘Tan’ because it was almost the only word he could say.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: About 12 cm long, it stores faeces until it’s convenient to empty it.

rounds.q: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal cords?
rounds.why: Lose both and the cords can’t open, which threatens the airway.
When you’re upright, inhaled food and fluid most often end up here.

rounds.q: Arnold’s nerve, supplying part of the ear canal, is a branch of which nerve?
rounds.why: Its auricular branch. That’s why cleaning some people’s ears makes them cough.
The brainstem runs breathing, heart rate and consciousness, and is the origin of most cranial nerves.
The spleen filters old red cells and fights infection. You can live without it, with vaccines and care.

rounds.q: Which is the smallest bone in the body?
rounds.why: About 3 mm long, in the middle ear. Shaped like a stirrup, which is what its name means.
It pumps blood to the lungs. Low pressure, so a much thinner wall than the left ventricle.
The iris is a ring of muscle that sets pupil size, and it gives eyes their colour.
The mandible is the only skull bone that moves. It’s also the strongest bone of the face.

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve is affected in Bell’s palsy?
rounds.why: Weakness of one whole side of the face, forehead included.
About 25 cm long. Food is pushed down it by waves of muscle, so you can swallow upside down.
It drains the head, neck and arms into the right atrium.
Strictly, the optic nerve is part of the brain itself, wrapped in the same layers (meninges).
Only the right lung has a middle lobe. The left lung’s lingula is its rough equivalent.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the thigh’s adductor muscles?
rounds.why: It leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen, the largest hole in the skeleton.
Between the right atrium and right ventricle. Three cusps, as the name says.

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of chewing?
rounds.why: Via its mandibular branch, V3: masseter, temporalis and both pterygoids.
Five vertebrae fused into one wedge, locking the spine into the pelvis.
Twelve vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs.
Three canals at right angles sense head rotation. Loose crystals in one cause BPPV.
About 25 cm long, curling around the head of the pancreas. Bile and pancreatic juice enter here.

rounds.q: Which is the longest bone in the body?
rounds.why: Roughly a quarter of your height.

rounds.q: Which nerve gives feeling to the highlighted palm-side area?
wrong: Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
rounds.why: The little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger. Pins and needles here after leaning on your elbow? Ulnar.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: It runs down the left side, fixed to the back wall of the abdomen.
It powers standing from a chair and climbing stairs.

rounds.q: Which bone doesn’t form a joint with any other bone?
rounds.why: It floats in the neck, held up by muscles and ligaments, anchoring the tongue.
It contains the fossa ovalis, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale. About a quarter of adults still have a small flap-like gap.
Its long spinous process is usually the first bump you feel at the base of the neck.
A cord-like band from femur to fibular head, separate from the joint capsule.
Surgeons can borrow latissimus as a flap for breast reconstruction, keeping this nerve and its artery.

rounds.q: Burning numbness on the outer thigh (meralgia paraesthetica). Which nerve?
rounds.answer: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
rounds.why: Often squeezed under the inguinal ligament by tight belts or weight gain.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted chamber of the inner ear.
rounds.why: It holds the utricle and saccule, which sense gravity and straight-line movement.
A clear gel filling the back of the eye. With age it shrinks and pulls away, giving floaters.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted spot on the retina.
rounds.why: A tiny pit packed with cones and no rods, for your sharpest vision. Faint stars look brighter if you look slightly to one side, onto the rods.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland’s secretions?
rounds.why: Via the lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion, then hitching a ride on the auriculotemporal nerve. The facial nerve just runs through the gland.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the short head of biceps femoris?
rounds.why: The only hamstring part not supplied by the tibial division.
Usually three cusps. About 1 to 2% of people have two (bicuspid), which can wear out early.
Longer and more horizontal than the right, because it has to pass under the aortic arch.
The muscly one that pumps blood to the whole body. Diagrams face you, so the patient’s left is on your right. Everyone falls for that once.
The pelvis carries your upper body’s weight onto the legs, and is wider and rounder in most women to allow for childbirth.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, your main breathing muscle?
rounds.why: ‘C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.’ It starts in the neck because the diaphragm began life up there in the embryo, then migrated down, dragging its nerve along.
Planning, personality and impulse control. In 1848 an iron rod shot through Phineas Gage’s frontal lobe; he survived, but friends said he was ‘no longer Gage’.
Several metres long, folded into a small space. Most nutrient absorption happens here.
Your biggest internal organ and a full-time chemistry lab. It can regrow from about a quarter of its tissue, which is why living donors can give a slice.
The thigh bone: your longest and strongest. It’s roughly a quarter of your height, which is how forensic teams estimate stature from a single bone.

rounds.q: You knock your ‘funny bone’. Which nerve just zapped you?
rounds.why: Not funny, not a bone. The ulnar nerve sits just under the skin behind the elbow, so a knock fires off tingles into your ring and little fingers.
Clear and flexible, it fine-tunes focus. It keeps adding layers all your life, like an onion, and slowly stiffens. Hello, reading glasses at 45.
The windpipe, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. The open back of each ‘C’ lets the oesophagus bulge forward when you swallow a big mouthful.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra. Count carefully.
rounds.why: The last thoracic vertebra, carrying the floating 12th rib. Counting up from L5 is quickest.

rounds.q: A ligament of Struthers, when present, can trap which nerve above the elbow?
rounds.why: Not to be confused with the arcade of Struthers, which can catch the ulnar nerve. Struthers liked naming things.

rounds.q: What is the sesamoid bone sometimes found in the lateral head of gastrocnemius?
rounds.why: Present in about a third of people. Once thought to be vanishing, it’s become more common over the past century.

rounds.q: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) mean which nerve is involved?
rounds.why: It’s the end of the nasociliary branch of V1, which also supplies the eye. Hence the warning sign for eye involvement.

rounds.q: Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle the hypoglossal doesn’t supply. What does?
rounds.why: It’s really a palate muscle moonlighting in the tongue, so it follows the palate’s nerve supply: the vagus.
The collarbone. It’s the first bone in the body to start hardening, around week five or six of pregnancy, and one of the most commonly broken bones in kids.

rounds.q: Wrist drop after a fracture of the humerus shaft. Which nerve?
rounds.why: The radial nerve hugs the humerus in the spiral groove. It extends the wrist and fingers.

rounds.q: Which nerve gives feeling to the highlighted palm-side area?
rounds.why: Thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger on the palm side. Squash it in the carpal tunnel and this zone tingles, often at night.
The thumb’s metacarpal is short, chunky and very mobile on the trapezium. That saddle joint gives you an opposable thumb.
Three to five tiny fused vertebrae: your vestigial tail.
